USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: At the Osaka G20 meeting, seek a truce that reopens negotiations and parks the unused List 4 (~$300B consumer-goods) hike without rolling back existing Section 301 tariffs or the Huawei Entity List. Insist that China return to the April draft’s legal/enforcement language on IP, forced tech transfer, and subsidies rather than State Council decrees. Do not concede purchases or unwind measures first; do not fire new tariffs into a weekend leaders’ meeting that both sides already scheduled to restart talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not existential. After China sent back the ~150-page draft with core legal commitments stripped (IP, tech transfer, competition, financial access, currency), the U.S. raised List 3 from 10% to 25% on May 10 and listed Huawei on May 16; China answered with higher duties on ~$60B of U.S. goods (many effective June 1), an unreliable-entity list, and a rare-earths signal. That package is already biting U.S. interests: USDA authorized up to $16B in farm aid after soybean exports to China collapsed (China fell from top ag market to fifth; ~90% drop in China-bound soy volume); flash manufacturing PMI printed 50.1 in early June (weakest since 2009) with two-thirds of manufacturers citing tariffs in input costs; 10-year yields fell from 2.69 (end-2018) to 2.05 and 2-year yields to 1.77 by June 26 as the Fed openly discussed cuts amid trade uncertainty. List 4 would land on phones, apparel, and other consumer goods and would likely kill talks (a person familiar with the talks said further tariffs would make talks “dead. Period.”). Opportunity remains: China’s industrial output growth slowed to the weakest pace since 2002, so leverage is not one-sided. That mix argues for a threat reading between neutral and the +0.5 “material drag / farm exposure” anchor, not for more escalation on the eve of a leaders’ meeting, and not for unilateral rollback after Beijing walked back the very structural terms that justified the 301 case. Negotiate without new commitments is the stance that keeps pressure on while using the June 18 Trump–Xi call and the already-agreed Osaka sit-down.
key_factors: May 2019 collapse of a near-complete draft after China deleted legal commitments on IP, tech transfer, and enforcement
List 3 already at 25% on ~$200B and Huawei Entity List in force; List 4 (~$300B consumer goods) proposed but not implemented
G20 Osaka Trump-Xi meeting already agreed (June 18 call); U.S. official goal is to reopen talks without accepting conditions on tariff use
Farm-belt retaliation: China soy purchases collapsed; USDA $16B aid package (May 23)
U.S. growth/financial stress: manufacturing PMI ~50.1, 10Y yield 2.05, Fed cut talk; China IP growth weakest since 2002 so leverage is two-sided

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets that negotiations are going "too slowly" and that China is attempting to "renegotiate." Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
Trump and Xi agree by phone to meet at the G20 in Osaka.
U.S. 10-year Treasury yield latest 2.05 on 2019-06-26, down 0.64 from 2.69 at end-2018 (~24% decline), with a sharp break after the May escalation.
U.S. 2-year yield latest 1.77 on 2019-06-26, down 0.71 from 2.48 (~29%), consistent with markets pricing Fed easing on trade/growth risk.

The United States hopes to re-launch trade talks after Trump and Xi meet in Japan, but will not accept conditions around U.S. use of tariffs; a person familiar said if they go with further tariffs, "the trade talks are dead. Period."
China returned a ~150-page draft riddled with reversals, deleting commitments to change laws on IP theft, forced tech transfer, competition policy, financial access, and currency.
USDA authorized up to $16 billion in programs in line with estimated impacts of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural goods.
IHS Markit U.S. manufacturing PMI declined to 50.1 in early June, lowest since September 2009; two-thirds of manufacturers attributed some or all raw-material cost increases to tariffs.
China’s industrial output growth slowed to the weakest pace since 2002, highlighting headwinds as it grapples with the U.S. tariff war.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the Osaka G20 meeting to reopen talks and seek a Buenos Aires-style freeze: no $300B List 4 tariffs, a pause in further entity-list expansion, and a return to working-level text without new structural or purchase commitments. Keep the unreliable-entity list and rare-earth signaling as unused leverage; do not populate the list or cut rare-earth exports on the eve of the summit. Do not unilaterally roll back the June 1 tariff hike or concede enforcement language the US claimed we walked back in May.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. After May 10 the US is already taxing ~$250B of our goods at 25%, and on May 16 Commerce put Huawei and affiliates on the Entity List; Google, Qualcomm and other US suppliers then cut Android/GMS and chips — a direct hit on our leading telecom/smartphone champion and on Made-in-China 2025 (timeline 2019-05-10, 2019-05-16, 2019-05-20). Official manufacturing PMI fell to 49.4 in May, new export orders to 46.5, and the employment sub-index to 47.0, the weakest since March 2009; April IP (5.4%) and retail sales (7.2%, slowest in 16 years) already showed the earlier stimulus rebound fading. That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor (export-sector damage, Huawei targeting, unemployment risk in export hubs). It is not +1.0: services PMI remains in expansion, March data showed stimulus can stabilize activity, and there is no visible financial-stability break. The residual opportunity (nationalist rally, faster tech autonomy, rare-earth leverage via Xi’s May 20 Jiangxi visit) is real but does not offset the tariff-plus-tech squeeze, so the net reading is +0.55 rather than negative.

Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. Trump has said he will decide the remaining ~$300B (phones, computers, clothing) after meeting Xi; Mnuchin has framed Osaka as analogous to Buenos Aires. Populating the unreliable-entity list or restricting rare earths now would give Washington a pretext to impose List 4 and deepen the Huawei cutoff — a second-order hit we cannot easily absorb given May factory and employment readings. Conversely, purchase or structural concessions before any US tariff freeze or Huawei relief would validate the May 5 “renegotiate” accusation and look like capitulation after a national-champion assault. Teams are already in contact to “consolidate the consensus” from the June 18 call. The disciplined stance is therefore near-zero on the escalate–concede axis: talk, freeze further damage, keep counters unused.
key_factors: US List 3 already at 25% on ~$200B plus $50B earlier lists; remaining ~$300B threatened after Osaka
Huawei Entity List plus Google/chip cutoff — firm-level tech assault, not just tariffs
May official PMI 49.4, export orders 46.5, manufacturing employment 47.0 (weakest since 2009)
G20 Osaka (28–29 Jun) is the first Trump-Xi meeting since the May collapse; US has tied List 4 to the meeting outcome
China already retaliated on ~$60B (1 Jun) and announced but has not implemented an unreliable-entity list — unused leverage
Talks previously stalled on enforcement/IP/tech-transfer, not just purchases; unilateral purchase concessions would be premature
